claim: New ages for flowstone, sediments and fossil bones from the Dinaledi Chamber are presented.
source: New ages for flowstone, sediments and fossil bones from the Dinaledi Chamber are presented.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that new ages are presented in the manuscript.

claim: Optically stimulated luminescence dating of sediments was combined with U-Th and palaeomagnetic analyses of flowstones.
source: We combined optically stimulated luminescence dating of sediments with U-Th and palaeomagnetic analyses of flowstones to establish that all sediments containing Homo naledi fossils can be allocated to a single stratigraphic entity (sub-unit 3b), interpreted to be deposited between 236 ka and 414 ka.
evidence: The abstract describes the dating methods used in the study.

claim: All sediments containing Homo naledi fossils can be allocated to a single stratigraphic entity (sub-unit 3b).
source: We combined optically stimulated luminescence dating of sediments with U-Th and palaeomagnetic analyses of flowstones to establish that all sediments containing Homo naledi fossils can be allocated to a single stratigraphic entity (sub-unit 3b), interpreted to be deposited between 236 ka and 414 ka.
evidence: The abstract states this conclusion based on the dating analyses performed.

claim: Sub-unit 3b was deposited between 236 ka and 414 ka.
source: We combined optically stimulated luminescence dating of sediments with U-Th and palaeomagnetic analyses of flowstones to establish that all sediments containing Homo naledi fossils can be allocated to a single stratigraphic entity (sub-unit 3b), interpreted to be deposited between 236 ka and 414 ka.
evidence: The abstract provides the age range for sub-unit 3b based on dating results.

claim: Three H. naledi teeth were dated with combined U-series and electron spin resonance (US-ESR) dating.
source: This result has been confirmed independently by dating three H. naledi teeth with combined U-series and electron spin resonance (US-ESR) dating.
evidence: The abstract describes the direct dating of fossil teeth.

claim: Two dating scenarios for the fossils were tested by varying the assumed levels of 222Rn loss in the encasing sediments.
source: Two dating scenarios for the fossils were tested by varying the assumed levels of 222Rn loss in the encasing sediments: a maximum age scenario provides an average age for the two least altered fossil teeth of 253 +82/–70 ka, whilst a minimum age scenario yields an average age of 200 +70/–61 ka.
evidence: The abstract describes the two scenarios used in age calculations.

claim: The maximum age scenario provides an average age for the two least altered fossil teeth of 253 +82/–70 ka.
source: Two dating scenarios for the fossils were tested by varying the assumed levels of 222Rn loss in the encasing sediments: a maximum age scenario provides an average age for the two least altered fossil teeth of 253 +82/–70 ka, whilst a minimum age scenario yields an average age of 200 +70/–61 ka.
evidence: The abstract provides the age estimate for the maximum age scenario.

claim: The minimum age scenario yields an average age of 200 +70/–61 ka.
source: Two dating scenarios for the fossils were tested by varying the assumed levels of 222Rn loss in the encasing sediments: a maximum age scenario provides an average age for the two least altered fossil teeth of 253 +82/–70 ka, whilst a minimum age scenario yields an average age of 200 +70/–61 ka.
evidence: The abstract provides the age estimate for the minimum age scenario.

claim: The maximum age scenario more closely reflects conditions in the cave, and therefore, the true age of the fossils.
source: We consider the maximum age scenario to more closely reflect conditions in the cave, and therefore, the true age of the fossils.
evidence: The abstract states the authors' interpretation of which scenario is more accurate.

claim: The depositional age of Homo naledi has been constrained to a period between 236 ka and 335 ka.
source: By combining the US-ESR maximum age estimate obtained from the teeth, with the U-Th age for the oldest flowstone overlying Homo naledi fossils, we have constrained the depositional age of Homo naledi to a period between 236 ka and 335 ka.
evidence: The abstract provides the final age range for H. naledi based on combined dating methods.

claim: Homo naledi survived into the later parts of the Pleistocene in Africa.
source: These age results demonstrate that a morphologically primitive hominin, Homo naledi, survived into the later parts of the Pleistocene in Africa, and indicate a much younger age for the Homo naledi fossils than have previously been hypothesized based on their morphology.
evidence: The abstract states this conclusion based on the age results.

claim: The age results indicate a much younger age for the Homo naledi fossils than have previously been hypothesized based on their morphology.
source: These age results demonstrate that a morphologically primitive hominin, Homo naledi, survived into the later parts of the Pleistocene in Africa, and indicate a much younger age for the Homo naledi fossils than have previously been hypothesized based on their morphology.
evidence: The abstract compares the new age results to previous hypotheses.

claim: The fossil assemblage attributed to Homo naledi from the Rising Star Cave represents one of the richest and most unusual taphonomic assemblages yet discovered in the hominin fossil record.
source: The fossil assemblage attributed to Homo naledi from the Rising Star Cave in the Cradle of Humankind, UNESCO World Heritage Area, South Africa (CoH) (Berger et al., 2015), represents one of the richest and most unusual taphonomic assemblages yet discovered in the hominin fossil record (Dirks et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction describes the significance of the fossil assemblage with citation to previous work.

claim: The remains are exceptionally well preserved and represent the largest collection of fossils from a single primitive hominin species ever discovered in Africa.
source: The remains are exceptionally well preserved and represent the largest collection of fossils from a single primitive hominin species ever discovered in Africa.
evidence: The introduction describes the preservation and significance of the fossil collection.

claim: The H. naledi fossils occur without a direct association with non-hominin macrofossil remains.
source: The H. naledi fossils occur without a direct association with non-hominin macrofossil remains, and are found deep inside the difficult to access U.W.101-Dinaledi Chamber (Dirks et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction describes the taphonomic context of the fossils with citation.

claim: The Dinaledi Chamber is characterised by a sedimentary environment that is geochemically and sedimentologically distinct from the rest of the Rising Star Cave.
source: The Dinaledi Chamber is characterised by a sedimentary environment that is geochemically and sedimentologically distinct from the rest of the Rising Star Cave (Dirks et al., 2015), and the fossiliferous deposit it contains is profoundly different from other known hominin-bearing cave assemblages in the CoH (e.g., Reynolds and Kibii, 2011; Dirks et al., 2010; Pickering et al., 2011a; Dirks and Berger, 2013; Bruxelles et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction describes the unique characteristics of the Dinaledi Chamber with citations.

claim: The fossiliferous deposit in the Dinaledi Chamber is profoundly different from other known hominin-bearing cave assemblages in the CoH.
source: The Dinaledi Chamber is characterised by a sedimentary environment that is geochemically and sedimentologically distinct from the rest of the Rising Star Cave (Dirks et al., 2015), and the fossiliferous deposit it contains is profoundly different from other known hominin-bearing cave assemblages in the CoH (e.g., Reynolds and Kibii, 2011; Dirks et al., 2010; Pickering et al., 2011a; Dirks and Berger, 2013; Bruxelles et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction compares the Dinaledi Chamber deposits to other sites with citations.

claim: The fossils occur as a dense bone accumulation in mostly unconsolidated muddy sediment that largely originated from within the cave through weathering of the dolomite host rock.
source: The fossils occur as a dense bone accumulation in mostly unconsolidated muddy sediment that largely originated from within the cave through weathering of the dolomite host rock (Dirks et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction describes the sedimentary context of the fossils with citation.

claim: The fossils have not been dated until now.
source: The fossils have not been dated until now.
evidence: The introduction states that this is the first dating study of the fossils.

claim: Dates were acquired via U-Th and ESR techniques using a double blind approach for each technique to ensure robust, reproducible results.
source: Dates acquired via U-Th and ESR techniques were obtained using a double blind approach for each technique to ensure robust, reproducible results, with each laboratory using their own analytical and computational approach.
evidence: The introduction describes the methodological approach to ensure reliability.

claim: The age of the hominins in the Dinaledi Chamber has implications for our understanding of the mode and tempo of the morphological evolution of hominins.
source: The age of the hominins in the Dinaledi Chamber has implications for our understanding of the mode and tempo of the morphological evolution of hominins (Hawks and Berger, 2016), raising questions about evolutionary stasis and the role of refugia.
evidence: The introduction discusses the broader implications of the age results with citation.

claim: The results challenge our ability to associate given hominin species to specific cultures and behaviours in the past.
source: The results challenge our ability to associate given hominin species to specific cultures and behaviours in the past.
evidence: The introduction discusses implications for understanding hominin behavior.

claim: The caves in the Cradle of Humankind (CoH), South Africa have yielded rich fossil assemblages of late Pliocene to early Pleistocene age.
source: The caves in the Cradle of Humankind (CoH), South Africa have yielded rich fossil assemblages of late Pliocene to early Pleistocene age, which include a range of hominin species (A. africanus, A. prometheus, A. sediba, P. robustus, H. ergaster, H. naledi and early Homo) and associated mammals, reptiles, and birds (e.g., Vrba, 1975, 1995; Brain, 1993; Tobias, 2000; Berger et al., 2010, 2015).
evidence: The geological setting section describes the fossil record of the region with citations.

claim: Rising Star Cave is situated in the Bloubank River valley, 2.2 km W of Sterkfontein Cave.
source: Rising Star Cave is situated in the Bloubank River valley, 2.2 km W of Sterkfontein Cave.
evidence: The geological setting section provides the geographic location of the cave.

claim: The cave system comprises several kilometres of mapped passageways.
source: The cave system comprises several kilometres of mapped passageways (Figure 1a) that are stratigraphically bound to a 20–30 m-thick, chert-poor dolomite horizon capped by a 1–1.3 m-thick chert unit that forms the roof to the cave system (Dirks et al., 2015).
evidence: The geological setting section describes the cave system with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: Geological mapping and laser-theodolite surveys indicate that the roof is intact and not penetrated by significant shafts that open to surface.
source: Geological mapping and laser-theodolite surveys indicate that this roof is intact and not penetrated by significant shafts that open to surface (Dirks et al., 2015; Kruger et al., 2016).
evidence: The geological setting section describes survey results with citations.

claim: The Dinaledi Chamber is ~30 m below surface and ~80 m in a straight line from the nearest present-day opening to the surface.
source: The Dinaledi Chamber, which contains most of the fossils of H. naledi, is ~30 m below surface and ~80 m in a straight line from the nearest present-day opening to the surface (Figure 1a).
evidence: The geological setting section provides the depth and distance measurements with figure reference.

claim: The main cavity forming the Dinaledi Chamber is ~15 m long with variable widths not exceeding 2.5 meters.
source: The main cavity forming the Dinaledi Chamber is ~15 m long with variable widths not exceeding 2.5 meters (Figure 1b), and expands near the intersection with a crosscutting passage, which is the location of the main excavation site to date (Figure 1b).
evidence: The geological setting section provides dimensions of the chamber with figure reference.

claim: There is no evidence that the present entrance into the Dinaledi Chamber has significantly changed since the deposition of the fossil hominins.
source: There is no evidence that the present entrance into the Dinaledi Chamber has significantly changed since the deposition of the fossil hominins, with sediment accumulating mostly near the current access point (Dirks et al., 2015, Dirks et al., 2016a; Figure 2).
evidence: The geological setting section describes the stability of the entrance with citations and figure reference.

claim: The oldest dated flowstone in the assemblage is Flowstone 1a overlying Unit 2, which yields age estimates of 502 +181/–53 ka (RS 23) and 478 +107/–41 ka (RS 22).
source: The oldest dated flowstone in the assemblage is Flowstone 1a overlying Unit 2, which yields age estimates of 502 +181/–53 ka (RS 23) and 478 +107/–41 ka (RS 22) (Table 1).
evidence: The U-Th dating results section provides age estimates with reference to a table.

claim: Flowstone samples that overlie sub-unit 3b yield age estimates that fall within four distinct time periods: ~242 ka, 88–106 ka, 50 ka, and 24–32 ka.
source: Flowstone samples that overlie sub-unit 3b, which contains the H. naledi fossils, yield age estimates that fall within four distinct time periods: ~242 ka (RS18 = 242 ± 5 ka [JCU] and 242.9 ± 6.6 ka [UoM]) for Flowstone 1c; 88–106 ka (RS1, RS8, RS13-17); 50 ka (RS6); and 24–32 ka (RS10, RS19-21) for Flowstone Group 2 deposits.
evidence: The U-Th dating results section provides age groupings for flowstones overlying fossil-bearing sediments.

claim: The results for RS18 provide a minimum age for the H. naledi fossils in this part of the cave.
source: The results for RS18 provide a minimum age for the H. naledi fossils in this part of the cave.
evidence: The U-Th dating results section interprets the stratigraphic significance of the RS18 age.

claim: Sample 1767 is an extremely worn upper premolar crown that is heavily weathered.
source: Sample 1767: This extremely worn upper premolar crown (Figure 6a) is heavily weathered, and only a small fragment of enamel was left attached to the dentine.
evidence: The U-Th analyses on teeth section describes the condition of sample 1767 with figure reference.

claim: Sample 1767 yields apparent U-Th ages of 44.5 ± 0.6 ka for dentine and 46.1 ± 0.7 ka for enamel.
source: Both dentine and enamel yield consistent results with apparent U-Th ages of 44.5 ± 0.6 ka for dentine and 46.1 ± 0.7 ka for enamel, and initial 234U/238U activity ratios at 6.99 ± 0.01 and 6.99 ± 0.04 respectively.
evidence: The U-Th analyses on teeth section provides age estimates for sample 1767.

claim: Sample 1788 is a lower right second molar that is well-preserved.
source: Sample 1788: This lower right second molar was covered by a thin layer of sediment and is well-preserved (Figure 6b).
evidence: The U-Th analyses on teeth section describes the condition of sample 1788 with figure reference.

claim: Sample 1810 is a lower left molar or premolar from the excavation pit that is near complete and only moderately weathered.
source: Sample 1810: This lower left molar or premolar from the excavation pit (Figures 4 and 6c), is near complete and only moderately weathered.
evidence: The U-Th analyses on teeth section describes the condition of sample 1810 with figure references.

claim: Sample 1841 is a baboon tooth that consists of an enamel crown that is structurally intact, but the enamel is friable and weathered.
source: Sample 1841 The baboon tooth consists of an enamel crown that is structurally intact, but the enamel is friable and weathered (Figure 7).
evidence: The U-Th analyses on teeth section describes the condition of sample 1841 with figure reference.

claim: Sample 1841 yields a mean apparent U-Th age estimate of 115.6 ± 1.9 ka with a mean initial 234U/238U activity ratio of 7.76 ± 0.05.
source: A recent U uptake event may have occurred affecting enamel in contact with sediment, resulting in a mean apparent U-Th age estimate of 115.6 ± 1.9 ka with a mean initial 234U/238U activity ratio of 7.76 ± 0.05 (Table 4).
evidence: The U-Th analyses on teeth section provides age estimates for sample 1841 with table reference.

claim: The results show that the teeth are older than 70 ka.
source: Collectively, the results show that the teeth are older than 70 ka, and considering sample 1810 with a minimum age of around 200 ka, that the H. naledi fossils are probably older than 200 ka (see Discussion).
evidence: The U-Th analyses on teeth section summarizes the age implications.

claim: Combined US-ESR ages determined by SCU for samples 1810, 1788 and 1767 under scenario 1 conditions are 284 ± 51 ka, 247 ± 41 ka and 104 ± 29 ka (2σ uncertainty), respectively.
source: Combined US-ESR ages determined by SCU for samples 1810, 1788 and 1767 under scenario 1 conditions (i.e., the maximum age scenario) are 284 ± 51 ka, 247 ± 41 ka and 104 ± 29 ka (2σ uncertainty), respectively (Table 7).
evidence: The US-ESR dating results section provides age estimates with table reference.

claim: Combined US-ESR ages determined by CENIEH-GU for samples 1810 and 1788 under scenario 1 conditions are 267 ± 68 ka and 211 ± 28 ka (2σ uncertainty), respectively.
source: Combined US-ESR ages determined by CENIEH-GU for samples 1810 and 1788 under scenario 1 conditions are 267 ± 68 ka and 211 ± 28 ka (2σ uncertainty), respectively (Table 7).
evidence: The US-ESR dating results section provides age estimates from a second laboratory with table reference.

claim: Results for sample 1767 are based on anomalously high (~20 times) U concentrations in enamel, and probably yield anomalously low age estimates.
source: Results for sample 1767 are based on anomalously high (~20 times) U concentrations in enamel, and probably yield anomalously low age estimates (Duval et al., 2012).
evidence: The US-ESR dating results section identifies a problem with sample 1767 with citation.

claim: Sample 1767 has been excluded from final age estimates.
source: This result is, therefore, considered to be unreliable and has been excluded from final age estimates (see Discussion).
evidence: The US-ESR dating results section states that sample 1767 was excluded.

claim: Together these results provide an age range of 139–335 ka for the H. naledi remains.
source: Together these results provide an age range of 139–335 ka for the H. naledi remains, although dating of flowstone encasing H. naledi bones helps to better constrain this range (see Discussion).
evidence: The US-ESR dating results section provides the overall age range.

claim: Combined US-ESR ages for the baboon tooth (sample 1841) determined by SCU using scenario 1 and 2 conditions are 723 ± 181 ka and 635 ± 148 ka respectively.
source: Combined US-ESR ages for the baboon tooth (sample 1841) determined by SCU using scenario 1 and 2 conditions are 723 ± 181 ka and 635 ± 148 ka respectively.
evidence: The US-ESR dating results section provides age estimates for the baboon tooth.

claim: The age results for sample 1841 provide an upper age limit for the deposition of the H. naledi bearing layer.
source: The age results provide an upper age limit for the deposition of the H. naledi bearing layer, and mark an earlier stage of deposition of mud clast breccia in the cave assigned to sub-unit 3a, which predates the entry of H. naledi fossils into the cave.
evidence: The US-ESR dating results section interprets the stratigraphic significance of the baboon tooth age.

claim: The MAM calculations for the three OSL samples yield maximum age estimates for the sediments of 231 ± 41 ka (OSL3), 241 ± 37 ka (OSL4), and 353 ± 61 ka (OSL5).
source: The MAM calculations for the three samples yield maximum age estimates for the sediments of 231 ± 41 ka (OSL3), 241 ± 37 ka (OSL4), and 353 ± 61 ka (OSL5).
evidence: The OSL dating results section provides age estimates using the MAM model.

claim: Phase A flowstone at the base of the palaeomagnetic sample records a consistent reversed magnetic polarity.
source: Phase A flowstone at the base of the sample records a consistent reversed magnetic polarity, with a clear overprint that is anti-parallel to the characteristic, reversed polarity remanence (ChRM) and is removed by ~10 mT.
evidence: The palaeomagnetic analysis results section describes the magnetic polarity of phase A.

claim: Phase B flowstone records a weak, normal polarity ChRM that is consistently isolated between 7 and 36mT.
source: Phase B flowstone records a weak, normal polarity ChRM that is consistently isolated between 7 and 36mT (Figure 13c).
evidence: The palaeomagnetic analysis results section describes the magnetic polarity of phase B with figure reference.

claim: Phase C flowstone also records a normal ChRM that is similar to that seen within phase B.
source: Phase C flowstone also records a normal ChRM that is similar to that seen within phase B (Figure 13c), although with slightly steeper inclinations (Figure 13c, Stereo Plot).
evidence: The palaeomagnetic analysis results section describes the magnetic polarity of phase C with figure reference.

claim: Three weathered bone fragments of H. naledi were analysed via radiocarbon dating at Beta Analytic Inc.
source: Three weathered bone fragments of H. naledi were analysed via radiocarbon dating at Beta Analytic Inc. (Florida, USA).
evidence: The radiocarbon dating results section describes the samples analyzed.

claim: Analyses indicated that no collagen was present in any of the samples and that the bone appeared possibly cremated.
source: Analyses indicated that no collagen was present in any of the samples and that the bone appeared possibly cremated.
evidence: The radiocarbon dating results section describes the condition of the bone samples.

claim: Tests did not support cremation and indicated that extensive secondary CaCO3 replacement had occurred, providing ages of 33.0 ± 0.2 ka and 35.50 ± 0.16 ka for two of the fragments.
source: Tests did not support cremation and indicated that extensive secondary CaCO3 replacement had occurred, providing ages of 33.0 ± 0.2 ka and 35.50 ± 0.16 ka for two of the fragments.
evidence: The radiocarbon dating results section provides age estimates and interpretation.

claim: The radiocarbon ages relate to late calcite precipitation in the bones that may reflect a wet period in the cave.
source: We interpret these ages to relate to late calcite precipitation in the bones that may reflect a wet period in the cave.
evidence: The radiocarbon dating results section interprets the meaning of the ages.

claim: U-Th dating of 17 flowstone samples has yielded minimum depositional age estimates for the sedimentary units they overlie.
source: U-Th dating of 17 flowstone samples (Figure 3) has yielded minimum depositional age estimates for the sedimentary units they overlie, and has provided insights into the timing of flowstone formation events (Tables 1, 2 and 3).
evidence: The discussion section summarizes the U-Th dating results with figure and table references.

claim: The most parsimonious age estimate for the H. naledi fossils is sometime between 236 ka and 335 ka.
source: Considering all age results presented here the most parsimonious age estimate for the H. naledi fossils is sometime between 236 ka and 335 ka.
evidence: The discussion section provides the final age estimate for the fossils.

claim: Until now, it has been generally assumed that morphologically primitive hominins like H. naledi did not survive into the later parts of the Pleistocene in Africa.
source: Until now, it has been generally assumed that morphologically primitive hominins like H. naledi (Berger et al., 2015) did not survive into the later parts of the Pleistocene in Africa.
evidence: The discussion section describes previous assumptions about hominin evolution with citation.

claim: The new age estimates for H. naledi show that an approximate age for the hominin fossil fragments cannot be simply deduced from their morphology.
source: The new age estimates for H. naledi show that an approximate age for the hominin fossil fragments cannot be simply deduced from their morphology (Thackeray, 2016; Dembo et al., 2016).
evidence: The discussion section discusses implications of the age results with citations.

claim: It is generally assumed that all African fossil hominins producing Middle Stone Age archaeological industries in the past 300 ka were part of a single variable species of early H. sapiens or an immediate precursor.
source: It is generally assumed that all African fossil hominins producing Middle Stone Age archaeological industries in the past 300 ka were part of a single variable species of early H. sapiens or an immediate precursor (e.g., Mcbrearty and Brooks, 2000; Lahr and Foley, 2001; Stringer, 2002).
evidence: The discussion section describes current assumptions about MSA tool makers with citations.

claim: The new ages now show that H. naledi existed at the same time as the first Middle Stone Age tools were produced in southern and eastern Africa.
source: The new ages now show that H. naledi existed at the same time as the first Middle Stone Age tools were produced in southern and eastern Africa, whilst skeletal evidence shows that H. naledi was probably capable of tool use (Berger et al., 2015; Hawks et al., 2017).
evidence: The discussion section discusses the temporal overlap between H. naledi and MSA tools with citations.

claim: This raises the possibility of H. naledi being responsible for some of the MSA traditions.
source: This raises the possibility of H. naledi being responsible for some of the MSA traditions.
evidence: The discussion section speculates about H. naledi's role in MSA tool production.
